title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 23
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Everything Under One Roof
passages.text:
A. Buying anything before the mid-nineteenth century involved a negotiation. Goods were kept behind a counter, prices were not displayed, what a customer paid depended on their apparent means and their skill at haggling, and entering a shop created an obligation to buy. The transaction was personal, slow and intimidating to anyone unsure of the conventions, which was a substantial part of the population.

B. The department store replaced all of this at once, and its innovations are easier to recognise now that they are universal. Goods were displayed openly and priced with a fixed marked figure; entry carried no obligation; returns were accepted. Each of these transferred a portion of the risk from the customer to the seller, and together they made shopping something that could be done by someone with no experience and no intention of buying.

C. The economics that made it possible were not obvious to contemporaries. A fixed low margin on a large volume returns more than a high margin on a small one, provided the volume actually arrives, and the store's scale was what allowed the margin to fall. Buying in quantity, selling many categories under one roof, and turning stock rapidly produced a cost structure that individual specialist shops could not match on price.

D. The social consequence most remarked on at the time concerned women. A large store was one of very few public places a woman of the middle classes could enter unaccompanied without comment, and stores understood this and built accordingly — tea rooms, reading rooms, cloakrooms and lavatories, which sound like amenities and functioned as permissions. The commercial motive was plain and the effect on public life was real regardless.

E. What was sold alongside the goods was the store itself. Elaborate buildings, lighting, window displays and seasonal spectacle cost a great deal and sold nothing directly; their purpose was to make the visit an event rather than an errand. This was the first large-scale demonstration that the setting of a purchase could be a product, an idea that has been reapplied continuously ever since and rarely credited to its origin.

F. The same logic explains the current difficulty. When the goods themselves are available elsewhere, more cheaply and without a journey, the reason to visit has to be the visit — and a business whose fixed costs are a large building in an expensive location cannot easily compete on the price of goods that a warehouse can ship. Stores that have survived have generally done so by becoming more like an event and less like a shop, which is a return to the original proposition rather than a departure from it.

passages.title: Listening to a Mountain
passages.text:
Volcanic eruptions are among the few large natural hazards that announce themselves in advance — not with a date, but with signals that something is coming — and those signals are given in a language that took a long time to learn to read. Magma moving upward through rock does not arrive silently: it fractures the material it displaces, deforms the surface above it, heats groundwater and releases gas, and each of these produces a signal that can be measured continuously from a distance.

Seismic monitoring does most of the work. Fracturing rock produces small earthquakes whose depth and character change as magma rises, and a shift from scattered brittle fracturing to sustained rhythmic tremor generally indicates fluid moving through a conduit rather than rock simply breaking. Networks around well-instrumented volcanoes now record events far too small to be felt, and the pattern over weeks matters more than any individual event.

Ground deformation provides an independent line. Satellite measurement can detect a flank swelling by centimetres over months, which indicates accumulation at depth, and the combination of inflation with changing seismicity is considerably more informative than either alone. Gas emissions supply a third: the ratio between gases released changes as magma approaches the surface, because different gases separate out at different pressures.

What monitoring cannot do is state when. The signals indicate that magma is moving and that the probability of eruption has risen sharply; they do not indicate whether the result will arrive in three days, three months or not at all, and unrest that subsides without eruption is common. This is the central operational difficulty, and it is a property of the system rather than a gap that better instruments will close.

The consequence is that the hard problem is not scientific. An evacuation ordered too early, followed by nothing, is expensive, disruptive and erodes the compliance that the next warning depends on; an evacuation ordered too late is catastrophic. The decision belongs to officials rather than scientists, is made under uncertainty that cannot be removed, and is judged afterwards against an outcome that was not knowable at the time.

The clearest lesson from the record concerns preparation rather than prediction. Places with rehearsed plans, established evacuation routes and populations who have been told in advance what the warning levels mean have evacuated successfully on short notice; places without them have not, regardless of how good the monitoring was. Instrumentation without an arrangement for acting on it produces excellent records of disasters that were fully anticipated.

passages.title: The Places That Cannot Absorb Us
passages.text:
Tourism is defended and attacked with the same statistic. It is among the largest employers in the world and a principal source of foreign earnings for many countries with few alternatives, and it concentrates large numbers of people in small, often fragile places whose residents did not choose the arrangement. Both statements are true, and the argument between them is usually conducted by people describing different places.

The economic case is strongest where alternatives are weakest. An island or a mountain region with little arable land, no minerals and a small domestic market has few routes to foreign earnings, and visitors are one of the few exports that can be sold without shipping anything. Employment is created at a range of skill levels, including for people whose formal qualifications are limited, which is not true of most other growth sectors.

The leakage that qualifies this case is substantial and unevenly reported. A large share of what a visitor spends may never enter the destination's economy, going instead to foreign-owned airlines, foreign-owned hotel groups and imported food and furnishings, and the share is highest exactly where dependence is highest — small economies that must import most of what a resort consumes. Headline tourism revenue and money actually retained can differ by a wide margin.

The costs that fall on residents are mostly not the ones visitors imagine. Crowding and litter are visible and comparatively minor; the durable damage is to housing, since accommodation let to visitors earns more than accommodation let to residents, and a market allowed to follow that gradient removes housing from the people who staff the industry. Water is the second: a visitor consumes several times what a resident does in places where supply is already the constraint.

Managing volume has proved harder than any other part of it. Charges levied on arrival raise revenue and change behaviour little at the price levels that are politically possible; caps on numbers work where there is a single controllable entry point and fail where there is not; and restrictions on new construction address the next decade rather than the present one. Nothing that has been tried reduces visitor numbers quickly without also removing the income that a substantial part of the population depends on.

The destinations that have managed the tension best have generally done so by deciding what they were selling before the market decided for them. Limiting the type of visitor rather than the number, taxing the activities that cause the damage rather than arrival in general, and reserving housing by rule rather than by price appear in most of the cases that have held together. These require deciding early, which is precisely when the pressure to decide is weakest.
